cues.text: Monasticism in Decline
By the early tenth century, Benedictine monasticism across Western Europe had suffered badly from Viking, Magyar, and Saracen raids.
It also suffered from the impoverishment and disorder of the late Carolingian world.
Lay lords treated abbeys as private property, installing relatives or favorites as abbots with little regard for the Rule of St. Benedict.
William the Pious's Donation
In 910, William I, Duke of Aquitaine , known as 'the Pious,' donated a hunting estate near the Grosne River in Burgundy.
The estate included vineyards, fields, mills, and woods, and was given to found a new Benedictine monastery dedicated to Sts. Peter and Paul .
He installed as its first abbot St. Berno , previously abbot of Gigny, entrusting him with a genuinely new form of governance.
Freedom from Secular and Episcopal Control

The founding charter of September 11, 910, contained an extraordinary provision: Cluny would be entirely free of William's own family and descendants, and placed directly under the protection of the Holy See rather than any local bishop or lord.
William deliberately surrendered the usual proprietary rights a founder retained over his monastery, asking only the monks' perpetual prayers for his soul in return.
A Centralized Reform

Under Berno and his remarkable successors, especially the long-reigned Abbot Odo (927–942), Cluny developed a stricter, more centralized observance of the Benedictine Rule, with an emphasis on solemn liturgy, learning, and independence from lay interference.

Unlike older Benedictine houses, each governed independently, new monasteries founded from or reformed by Cluny remained subject to the abbot of Cluny himself, creating something close to a single unified order avant la lettre.
Spread Across Europe

Over the following two centuries the Cluniac reform spread rapidly through France, Italy, Spain, England, and the German lands, either through new foundations or the absorption of existing, decayed houses.

By the time of its greatest abbots, such as St. Hugh of Cluny in the eleventh century, the Congregation of Cluny numbered well over a thousand dependent priories, and its abbey church was, for a time, the largest in Christendom.
Legacy
Cluny's reform is widely credited with reviving the moral and spiritual vigor of Western monasticism after its Carolingian-era decline.

It is also credited with training many churchmen who later drove the broader eleventh-century Gregorian Reform against simony and lay investiture, including Pope Urban II, who would launch the First Crusade in 1095.
Cluny remains the paradigm example of how a single, well-governed foundation could reshape the religious life of an entire continent.
